This notebook analyzes how residential electricity consumption changes when
homes switch from fossil-fuel heating to heat pumps. It answers questions like
"how much does the typical home's annual load double?" and "how much does
winter load triple?" — with the full distribution, not just averages.

The functions doing the data crunching live in
[`lib/rates_analysis/load_profile_funcs.py`](../../../lib/rates_analysis/load_profile_funcs.py),
a module parameterized by state/batch/segment so it can be reused for any
utility in any state. This notebook just calls those functions with
CT Eversource-specific values.

**To adapt this notebook to another state or utility**, change only the
Parameters section below and the winter/summer month definitions.

## Setup

```{python}
#| label: setup

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path
from typing import cast

import polars as pl
import yaml
from great_tables import GT

from lib.plotnine import SB_COLORS, theme_switchbox
from lib.great_tables import get_switchbox_gt_tab_options
from lib.quarto import display_figure, display_gt
from lib.rates_analysis.rate_case_funcs import (
    HEATING_ORDER,
    HEATING_TYPE_LABELS,
    MONTH_ORDER,
    add_heating_label,
    load_master_bills,
    segment_name,
    weighted_mean,
    weighted_quantile,
)
from lib.rates_analysis.load_profile_funcs import (
    build_load_profile_base,
    build_peak_kw_base,
    load_profile_summary,
    plot_annual_kwh_hist,
    plot_before_after_scatter,
    plot_dumbbell_summary,
    plot_incremental_kw_hist,
    plot_incremental_kwh_hist,
    plot_multiplier_bar,
    plot_outcome_spread,
    plot_pct_change_hist,
    plot_pct_change_vs_base_load,
)
```

## Parameters

Everything below this section is derived from these inputs. To run this
notebook for a different state or utility, change only these values.

```{python}
#| label: params

_batch_config = yaml.safe_load(Path("../batch_config.yaml").read_text())

STATE = _batch_config["STATE"]
BATCH = _batch_config["BATCH"]
ELECTRIC_UTILITY = "ct_eversource"
UTILITY_LABEL = "Eversource CT"

# Segment names: precalc = baseline population (upgrade 0),
# calibrated = same buildings modeled with heat pumps (upgrade 2).
BASELINE_SCENARIO = _batch_config["BASELINE_BILL_SCENARIO"]
SEG_BEFORE = segment_name(BASELINE_SCENARIO, "precalc")
SEG_AFTER = segment_name(BASELINE_SCENARIO, "calibrated")

# Seasonal definitions: winter is November–March for CT Eversource
# (Rate 6 heating season, Exhibit CLP-RATES-1). Summer is everything else.
WINTER_MONTH_NUMS = [11, 12, 1, 2, 3]
SUMMER_MONTH_LABELS: set[str] = {
    MONTH_ORDER[m - 1] for m in range(1, 13) if m not in WINTER_MONTH_NUMS
}
WINTER_MONTH_LABELS: set[str] = {MONTH_ORDER[m - 1] for m in WINTER_MONTH_NUMS}

print(f"state={STATE}  batch={BATCH}  utility={ELECTRIC_UTILITY}")
print(f"seg_before={SEG_BEFORE}  seg_after={SEG_AFTER}")
print(f"winter={sorted(WINTER_MONTH_LABELS)}  summer={sorted(SUMMER_MONTH_LABELS)}")
```

## Import data

We load CAIRO's master bills for two segments of the same scenario:

- **Precalc** (upgrade 0): today's mixed population with their existing
  heating systems. `elec_grid_kwh` reflects current electricity usage.
- **Calibrated** (upgrade 2): the same buildings modeled as if they had
  heat pumps. `elec_grid_kwh` reflects post-HP electricity usage.

Joining on `bldg_id` gives us the before/after kWh for every building.
Fuel-type labels (natural gas, oil/propane, electric resistance) always come
from the baseline (upgrade 0) metadata, so they describe what the home heated
with *before* the heat pump.

```{python}
#| label: ingest

profiles = build_load_profile_base(
    STATE,
    BATCH,
    SEG_BEFORE,
    SEG_AFTER,
    summer_month_labels=SUMMER_MONTH_LABELS,
    electric_utility=ELECTRIC_UTILITY,
)

print(f"Buildings loaded: {profiles.height:,}")
print(f"Columns: {profiles.columns}")
profiles.head(5)
```

Let's see how many buildings we have by baseline heating type, and what their
average annual electricity consumption looks like before and after heat pumps.

```{python}
#| label: population-overview

summary = load_profile_summary(profiles)
summary
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-population-overview
#| tbl-cap: "Population overview: weighted-mean kWh by baseline heating type"

_tbl = (
    summary.select(
        pl.col("group").alias("Heating type"),
        pl.col("n_unweighted").alias("Buildings (unweighted)"),
        pl.col("n_weighted").cast(pl.Int64).alias("Households (weighted)"),
        pl.col("mean_annual_kwh_before").round(0).cast(pl.Int64).alias("Annual kWh (before)"),
        pl.col("mean_annual_kwh_after").round(0).cast(pl.Int64).alias("Annual kWh (after)"),
        pl.col("multiplier_annual").alias("Annual multiplier"),
        pl.col("multiplier_winter").alias("Winter multiplier"),
        pl.col("multiplier_summer").alias("Summer multiplier"),
    )
)

gt_tbl = (
    GT(_tbl.to_pandas())
    .tab_header(title=f"Load profile summary: {UTILITY_LABEL}")
    .fmt_number(columns=["Buildings (unweighted)", "Households (weighted)", "Annual kWh (before)", "Annual kWh (after)"], decimals=0, use_seps=True)
    .fmt_number(columns=["Annual multiplier", "Winter multiplier", "Summer multiplier"], decimals=2)
    .tab_options(**get_switchbox_gt_tab_options())
)
display_gt(gt_tbl)
```

## Annual electricity consumption

### All homes by baseline fuel

The first chart shows how the full distribution of annual electricity
consumption shifts when homes install heat pumps. Each panel (Before / After)
shows the weighted histogram, with bars colored by baseline heating fuel.

The rightward shift in the "After" panel — especially the long right tail —
shows the increased electricity usage from heat pump heating. Natural-gas homes
(dark blue) tend to start with lower electricity consumption and shift the most.

```{python}
#| label: fig-annual-kwh-hist-all
#| fig-cap: "Annual electricity consumption before and after heat pump installation, by baseline heating fuel"

plot_annual_kwh_hist(profiles, x_max=50_000)
```

### By fuel type

Now the same chart filtered to each major fuel group, so we can see the
shape of each distribution without the others overlapping.

```{python}
#| label: fig-annual-kwh-hist-natgas
#| fig-cap: "Annual electricity consumption: natural-gas-heated homes"

plot_annual_kwh_hist(profiles, fuel_filter="natgas", x_max=40_000)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-annual-kwh-hist-delivered
#| fig-cap: "Annual electricity consumption: oil/propane-heated homes"

plot_annual_kwh_hist(profiles, fuel_filter="delivered_fuels", x_max=40_000)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-annual-kwh-hist-er
#| fig-cap: "Annual electricity consumption: electric-resistance-heated homes"

plot_annual_kwh_hist(profiles, fuel_filter="electrical_resistance", x_max=40_000)
```

### Before vs. after scatter

Each dot is one building. The x-axis is the building's annual kWh before the
heat pump, and the y-axis is after. Buildings above the dashed diagonal line
use more electricity after installation (which is most of them — heat pumps
run on electricity). The farther above the line, the bigger the increase.

This chart captures the full story in one glance: the level, the spread,
and the relationship between starting point and ending point.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scatter-annual
#| fig-cap: "Annual kWh before vs. after heat pump, by baseline heating fuel"

display_figure(plot_before_after_scatter(profiles, "annual", axis_max=50_000))
```

### Percent change vs. baseline load

Does the percent change in electricity consumption depend on how much a home
used before the heat pump? This scatter puts baseline annual kWh on the x-axis
and percent change on the y-axis, faceted by fuel type.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pct-vs-base-annual
#| fig-cap: "Annual percent change in electricity vs. baseline consumption, by heating fuel"

display_figure(plot_pct_change_vs_base_load(profiles, "annual", x_max=30_000, y_range=(-0.5, 10.0)))
```

### Outcome spread vs. baseline load

The scatter above suggests that homes with higher baseline electricity may
show more variable outcomes. This chart confirms it: for each 1,000 kWh
bin of baseline consumption, the shaded ribbon spans the interquartile range
(Q25–Q75) of percent change, and the line is the weighted median. If the
ribbon widens to the right, outcome variance increases with baseline load.

```{python}
#| label: fig-outcome-spread-annual
#| fig-cap: "IQR of annual percent change in electricity, by baseline consumption and heating fuel"

plot_outcome_spread(profiles, "annual", x_max=30_000)
```

### Dumbbell: mean annual kWh by fuel type

Each row shows one fuel type's weighted-mean annual kWh. The dark dot is
"before," the light dot is "after," and the number above is the multiplier.
This is the simplest possible answer to "how much does the load change?"

```{python}
#| label: fig-dumbbell-annual
#| fig-cap: "Mean annual electricity consumption before and after heat pump, by baseline heating fuel"

display_figure(plot_dumbbell_summary(summary, "annual"))
```

### Multiplier bar chart

The same multipliers from the dumbbell chart, but broken out by season. This
directly answers the question "your annual load doubles and your winter load
triples" — with the actual numbers.

```{python}
#| label: fig-multiplier-bar
#| fig-cap: "Electricity consumption multiplier (after / before) by fuel type and season"

plot_multiplier_bar(summary)
```

## Summer electricity consumption

Heat pumps are also air conditioners, and high-efficiency ones at that. For
homes that already had central air conditioning, summer electricity consumption
often *decreases* slightly after switching to a heat pump. For homes without
prior cooling, summer may increase (they gain air conditioning for the first
time).

### Percent change in summer kWh

```{python}
#| label: fig-pct-change-summer-all
#| fig-cap: "Percent change in summer electricity consumption after heat pump, by baseline fuel"

plot_pct_change_hist(profiles, "summer", x_max=2.0)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pct-change-summer-natgas
#| fig-cap: "Percent change in summer electricity consumption: natural-gas-heated homes"

plot_pct_change_hist(profiles, "summer", fuel_filter="natgas", x_max=2.0)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pct-change-summer-delivered
#| fig-cap: "Percent change in summer electricity consumption: oil/propane-heated homes"

plot_pct_change_hist(profiles, "summer", fuel_filter="delivered_fuels")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pct-change-summer-er
#| fig-cap: "Percent change in summer electricity consumption: electric-resistance-heated homes"

plot_pct_change_hist(profiles, "summer", fuel_filter="electrical_resistance")
```

## Winter electricity consumption

Winter is where the action is. When a home switches from a gas furnace or oil
boiler to a heat pump, virtually all of the heating load moves to the electric
meter. The winter electricity consumption increase is the dominant driver of
the annual load change.

### Percent change in winter kWh

```{python}
#| label: fig-pct-change-winter-all
#| fig-cap: "Percent change in winter electricity consumption after heat pump, by baseline fuel"

plot_pct_change_hist(profiles, "winter", x_max=10.0)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pct-change-winter-natgas
#| fig-cap: "Percent change in winter electricity consumption: natural-gas-heated homes"

plot_pct_change_hist(profiles, "winter", fuel_filter="natgas", x_max=10.0)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pct-change-winter-delivered
#| fig-cap: "Percent change in winter electricity consumption: oil/propane-heated homes"

plot_pct_change_hist(profiles, "winter", fuel_filter="delivered_fuels", x_max=10.0)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pct-change-winter-er
#| fig-cap: "Percent change in winter electricity consumption: electric-resistance-heated homes"

plot_pct_change_hist(profiles, "winter", fuel_filter="electrical_resistance")
```

### Before vs. after scatter (winter only)

The winter scatter shows the relationship even more dramatically than the
annual one — the cloud of points is well above the diagonal for gas and
oil/propane homes, reflecting the 2-4x increase in winter kWh.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scatter-winter
#| fig-cap: "Winter kWh before vs. after heat pump, by baseline heating fuel"

display_figure(plot_before_after_scatter(profiles, "winter", axis_max=40_000))
```

### Dumbbell: mean winter kWh by fuel type

```{python}
#| label: fig-dumbbell-winter
```

## Incremental kWh

The incremental kWh is the absolute increase in electricity consumption
(after minus before). Unlike percent change, it shows the actual volume of
new load — which matters for infrastructure planning and cost allocation.

### Annual incremental kWh

```{python}
#| label: fig-incremental-kwh-annual-all
#| fig-cap: "Incremental annual kWh after heat pump, by baseline heating fuel"

plot_incremental_kwh_hist(profiles, "annual", x_range=(-8_000, 8_000))
```

### Summer incremental kWh

```{python}
#| label: fig-incremental-kwh-summer-all
#| fig-cap: "Incremental summer kWh after heat pump, by baseline heating fuel"

plot_incremental_kwh_hist(profiles, "summer", x_range=(-6_000, 6_000))
```

### Winter incremental kWh

```{python}
#| label: fig-incremental-kwh-winter-all
#| fig-cap: "Incremental winter kWh after heat pump, by baseline heating fuel"

plot_incremental_kwh_hist(profiles, "winter")
```

## Incremental peak demand (kW)

Peak demand (the single highest hour of electricity consumption) matters for
distribution and transmission capacity planning. Here we look at how each
building's peak kW changes after installing a heat pump.

For CT Eversource, the system peak is in summer, but residential heat pump
peaks occur in winter. The winter incremental peak is the most policy-relevant
metric for understanding future infrastructure needs.

```{python}
#| label: load-peak-kw

peak_kw = build_peak_kw_base(
    STATE,
    ELECTRIC_UTILITY,
    BATCH,
    SEG_BEFORE,
    SEG_AFTER,
    summer_month_labels=SUMMER_MONTH_LABELS,
    weights=profiles.select("bldg_id", "weight"),
)
heating_labels = profiles.select("bldg_id", "heating_type_v2", "heating_label")

print(f"Buildings with hourly data: {peak_kw.height:,}")
```

### Annual incremental peak kW

```{python}
#| label: fig-incremental-kw-annual
#| fig-cap: "Incremental annual peak kW after heat pump, by baseline heating fuel"

plot_incremental_kw_hist(peak_kw, "annual", heating_labels=heating_labels)
```

### Summer incremental peak kW

```{python}
#| label: fig-incremental-kw-summer
#| fig-cap: "Incremental summer peak kW after heat pump, by baseline heating fuel"

plot_incremental_kw_hist(peak_kw, "summer", heating_labels=heating_labels)
```

### Winter incremental peak kW

```{python}
#| label: fig-incremental-kw-winter
#| fig-cap: "Incremental winter peak kW after heat pump, by baseline heating fuel"

plot_incremental_kw_hist(peak_kw, "winter", heating_labels=heating_labels)
```

## Summary statistics

```{python}
#| label: tbl-summary-stats
#| tbl-cap: "Detailed load profile statistics by baseline heating type"

_detail = summary.select(
    pl.col("group").alias("Heating type"),
    pl.col("n_unweighted").alias("n"),
    pl.col("mean_annual_kwh_before").round(0).cast(pl.Int64).alias("Annual kWh before"),
    pl.col("mean_annual_kwh_after").round(0).cast(pl.Int64).alias("Annual kWh after"),
    (pl.col("multiplier_annual")).alias("Annual mult."),
    pl.col("mean_winter_kwh_before").round(0).cast(pl.Int64).alias("Winter kWh before"),
    pl.col("mean_winter_kwh_after").round(0).cast(pl.Int64).alias("Winter kWh after"),
    (pl.col("multiplier_winter")).alias("Winter mult."),
    pl.col("mean_summer_kwh_before").round(0).cast(pl.Int64).alias("Summer kWh before"),
    pl.col("mean_summer_kwh_after").round(0).cast(pl.Int64).alias("Summer kWh after"),
    (pl.col("multiplier_summer")).alias("Summer mult."),
    (pl.col("mean_pct_change_winter") * 100).round(0).alias("Winter Δ% (mean)"),
    (pl.col("median_pct_change_winter") * 100).round(0).alias("Winter Δ% (median)"),
)

gt_detail = (
    GT(_detail.to_pandas())
    .tab_header(title=f"Load profile statistics: {UTILITY_LABEL}")
    .fmt_number(columns=["n", "Annual kWh before", "Annual kWh after", "Winter kWh before", "Winter kWh after", "Summer kWh before", "Summer kWh after"], decimals=0, use_seps=True)
    .fmt_number(columns=["Annual mult.", "Winter mult.", "Summer mult."], decimals=2)
    .fmt_number(columns=["Winter Δ% (mean)", "Winter Δ% (median)"], decimals=0, pattern="{x}%")
    .tab_options(**get_switchbox_gt_tab_options())
)
display_gt(gt_detail)
```
